findings.title: SHA-256 padded-length comparator does not actually bound paddedInLength
findings.evidence: Sha256General (lines 125-128) and Sha256Partial (lines 237-240) treat paddedInLength as a free field element but validate it only with `component bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits); bitLengthVerifier.in[0] <== paddedInLength; bitLengthVerifier.in[1] <== maxBitLength; bitLengthVerifier.out === 1;`. circomlib LessEqThan/LessThan merely proves that `in[0] + 2^(n+1) - (in[1]+1)` has bit n+1 clear after a field subtraction; it assumes both inputs are already n-bit range constrained, and paddedInLength never is. A prover sets paddedInLength just below the BN254 modulus p (for example p-512) so the modular subtraction wraps, the high bit reads 0, and `bitLengthVerifier.out === 1` holds even though paddedInLength is vastly larger than maxBitLength. The witness is reachable directly through the public inputs of Sha256Bytes/Sha256BytesPartial, which forward it unmodified via `sha.paddedInLength <== paddedInLength * 8`, so any consumer using this SHA template as a library primitive (without its own external length range check) is affected. This is the length-comparator weakness that makes the out-of-range block selector reachable.

findings.title: Attacker-chosen block index drives array selector out of range, forcing an all-zero SHA-256 output
findings.evidence: `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` (line 110; line 233 in Sha256Partial) is a non-constrained witness assignment, and the same value is used as the array selector at `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195; line 292 in Sha256Partial). The floor verifiers that would pin inBlockIndex are commented out (lines 114-122/241-...), and the only tie is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111), which is modular. Combining the two issues: choose paddedInLength = p - 512, which passes the (bypassable) length comparator, then inBlockIndex = (p-512)*512^-1 mod p = p-1 so index = p-2, which is outside [0, maxBlocks) yet still accepted by ItemAtIndex's LessThan guard (array.circom line 28). No equality flag matches, so ItemAtIndex's `out <== calcTotal.sum` returns 0 for every bit and the prover obtains out[256] = all zeros, a SHA-256 value independent of the supplied paddedIn, breaking the binding of the gadget. The audit report notes this is exploitable for the standalone/library template; in the full EmailVerifier the extra AssertZeroPadding constraints on header/body lengths make the malicious length hard to satisfy, so end-to-end exploitation is narrower.

findings.title: ItemAtIndex index check is bypassable because index is not range constrained
findings.evidence: `component lessThan = LessThan(bitLength); lessThan.in[0] <== index; lessThan.in[1] <== maxArrayLen; lessThan.out === 1;` (lines 25-28) is the only guard enforcing index < maxArrayLen, but index is a witness-supplied field element with no Num2Bits/range constraint. circomlib LessThan(n) only proves `in[0] + 2^n - in[1]` fits in n+1 bits, so a malicious index near the field modulus (e.g. index = p-2) makes the subtraction wrap to a small value, yields out === 1, and is accepted. The equality indicators `eqs[i]` then never match a valid position, so `out <== calcTotal.sum` silently returns 0 instead of rejecting the witness. This is the comparator Sha256General/Sha256Partial depend on (sha.circom lines 191 and 288) to select the correct compression block; the sound construction proves uniqueness with `sum_i eq(index,i) === 1`.
